name: Northern Akhvakh
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Creissels, Denis. 2018. A sketch of Northern Akhvakh (2nd draft, revised August 2018), submitted for Koryakov, Y., Y. Lander & T. Maisak (eds.), The Caucasian Languages: An International Handbook. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton (HSK). 36 pp. [Glottolog: Creissels 2020]; supplemented by Creissels, Denis. 2010. The accentuation of Northern Akhvakh nouns in the nominative case. Paper, conference 'Kavkazskie jazyki: geneticheskie, areal'nye svjazi i tipologicheskie obshchnosti', Makhachkala, 17-18 June 2010. 7 pp.
catalog_locator: Sketch sec. 2.4 'Prosody', draft pp. 5-6; fn. 11; 2010 paper secs. 2-5, pp. 1-6
catalog_quote: Contrary to Kodzasov’s (1999) claim, Northern Akhvakh is NOT a tone language. Northern Akhvakh is a typical word accent language in that, with the exception of morphologically complex words whose prosodic pattern may include secondary accents, the number of possible prosodic patterns for words with a given number of syllables never exceeds the number of syllables: there are two possible patterns for two-syllable word forms, three for three-syllable word forms, etc. What is however atypical is the realization of one of the possible patterns: in isolation, Northern Akhvakh word forms may show, either an accent on a non-final syllable, or no perceptible accentual contrast at all (which can therefore be analyzed as the realization of a word-final accent). [Creissels 2010, pp. 2, 4] disyllabic nouns have two possible accent patterns: ó o (with an accent on the 1st syllable) and o o (accentless) ... it seems to me preferable to posit that the accentual patterns observed in isolation directly reflect the accentual structure of words as determined by the interaction of lexical information and morphological rules, and that rules conditioned by syntactic structure and / or information structure may introduce additional accents attached to the last syllable of words.
world_status: statement found in an open source

Title page: 'A sketch of Northern Akhvakh (2nd draft, revised August 2018)', Denis Creissels, submitted for the Koryakov/Lander/Maisak HSK handbook. Sec. 2.4 'Prosody' (the text layerdraft pp. 5-6) contains the quoted passage word for word: 'Contrary to Kodzasov's (1999) claim, Northern Akhvakh is NOT a tone language. Northern Akhvakh is a typical word accent language in that, with the exception of morphologically complex words whose prosodic pattern may include secondary accents, the number of possible prosodic patterns for words with a given number of syllables never exceeds the number of syllables: there are two possible patterns for two-syllable word form…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent, not tone; its position is not phonologically predictable: an n-syllable word has n possible patterns (accent on any non-final syllable, or 'accentless' = flat low contour, analysable as final accent), the choice being fixed by the lexicon and by morphological rules (Creissels 2010: e.g. disyllabic nouns are lexically either initial-accented or accentless; -Ca plural suffixes add an accent on the stem-final syllable, vowel-change plurals delete the lexical accent; stress alone distinguishes -wa perfective w-óq'-u-wa from potential w-oq'-ú-wa). Older first-hand sources characterise the same variety differently: Magomedbekova 1999: 254 'stress weak, dynamic, non-fixed'; Kodzasov (Kibrik & Kodzasov 1990: 323, same village Tad-Magitl') 'word stress absent, phrasal accent usually on the 1st syllable, syllabic tones H/L/R/F'. All three agree there is no fixed stress position.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary accents only in morphologically complex words (sketch 2.4); Creissels 2010 pp. 5-6: when an accent-adding plural suffix attaches to a lexically accented noun both accents are retained (χ̄ṹk’ače -> χ̄ṹk’ačéla), with fluctuating relative prominence when adjacent (ráʁíla).
new_statements.exceptions: Accentless word class (no perceptible accent in isolation); context-conditioned final accent (e.g. es̄e vs es̄é 'our' depending on whether the following noun has initial accent, Creissels 2010 p. 4); a few nouns keep their accent in vowel-change plurals (ák’a -> ák’o 'woman', q̄’ačáʁa -> q̄’ačáʁo); Kodzasov's competing tonal analysis explicitly rejected as allophonic.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent as realised on word forms in isolation (citation forms); Creissels notes that syntactic / information-structure rules may add an accent on the last syllable of words in context, and Kodzasov 1990 speaks of phrasal accent on the 1st syllable. Variety: Northern Akhvakh, speakers from Tadmagitl' (and Lologonitl', Sovetskoe, Kamyškutan) = akhv1239 proper.
new_statements.identity_note: All three first-hand sources describe Northern Akhvakh proper (akhv1239): Creissels' data are from Tadmagitl', Lologonitl', Sovetskoe and Kamyškutan speakers (plus separate work on Axaxdərə Akhvakh in Azerbaijan, also Northern); Kodzasov's sketch is explicitly 's. Tad-Magitli'; Magomedbekova 1999 states her sketch uses Northern-dialect data. Southern Akhvakh (Cegob, Tljanub, Ratlub; sout3220-type varieties) is not covered by any of the statements.

tone_statements.citation: Kodzasov, Sandro V. 2003. Towards an evolutionary typology of stress. In: Proceedings of the 15th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences (ICPhS), Barcelona, 63-66.
tone_statements.quote: Also most languages of the Northern group lack stress. Only three languages (among 14) display pronounced stress. These are Avar which functions as lingua franca of the whole region, Godoberi and Chamalal. [...] Supposedly, the stiff/slack opposition in these languages goes back to tonal contrasts. And some languages of the Northern subgroup (Akhwakh, Andi) have syllabic tones. The presence of tones in Akhwakh has received an experimental confirmation.
tone_statements.locator: p. 64, section on Daghestanian languages, right column
tone_statements.summary: Areal claim only: Northern-group Daghestanian mostly stressless, stiff/slack register opposition of tonal origin, true syllabic tone in Andi/Akhvakh; nothing specific to Botlikh.

sources.note: Whole paper on accent (corpus of ~3600 sentences, speaker I. Abdulaeva): contrast accented/unaccented syllables can be as sharp as in Russian or Spanish; accented words (accent on a non-final syllable) coexist with accentless words (flat, low contour); disyllabic nouns ó o or accentless, trisyllabic ó o o / o ó o / accentless (pp. 2-3); accent placement = lexical information + morphological rules (p. 4); plural suffixes -Ca add an accent on the stem-final syllable, vowel-change plurals delete the lexical accent, two accents may co-occur (pp. 5-6); syntactic/information-structure rules may add…

sources.note: States that most Northern-group Daghestanian languages lack stress, only Avar, Godoberi and Chamalal have pronounced stress, the stiff/slack vocalic opposition 'supposedly goes back to tonal contrasts', and Andi and Akhwakh have syllabic tones (Akhwakh experimentally confirmed). By implication Botlikh falls in the 'lack stress' majority, which conflicts with Gudava/Magomedbekova's 'weak dynamic mobile stress'; Botlikh itself is not discussed.
